result.markdown: --- title: "W13 Lab: Start-to-finish LVPA runbook (Holzinger & Swineford)" date: today description: 'Download .qmd' data: 'Built into lavaan: HolzingerSwineford1939' format: html --- ## Purpose Run a complete latent variable path analysis (LVPA) the way you would for a real project: 1. Understand the study and the data. 2. Fit and evaluate the **measurement model** (CFA). 3. Decide whether to modify it, and whether to move on with the structural model. 4. Fit and evaluate the **structural model**. 5. Answer the research question. **What is given:** the code structure (fitting, fit indices, output tables, diagrams). **What you do:** - write every model yourself (lavaan syntax), - decide whether the model fit is acceptable and say why, - decide whether to change the model based on modification indices, - decide whether to proceed from the measurement to the structural model, - read the structural output and respond to the research question, based on the outputs. ## About the standard errors Standard errors, p-values and confidence intervals here come from the **bootstrap** (1,000 resamples of the students), not from the default formulas. Bootstrapping does not assume the data are normal. The confidence intervals are **percentile** intervals. Fitting takes a little longer (about 20 seconds per model). The fit indices (chi-square, CFI, RMSEA, SRMR) are unaffected by this choice. ## How this file works Only edit the three chunks marked `# YOUR TURN`. Each of those chunks starts with a **placeholder model** (every variable just gets a residual variance). The placeholder is meaningless, but it is valid, so the whole file runs from top to bottom before you write anything. The results only mean something once you replace the placeholder with your own model. Type your decisions and reasoning in the **Your response** spaces. --- # The study **Source.** Holzinger and Swineford (1939), *A study in factor analysis: The stability of a bifactor solution*, Supplementary Educational Monographs, No. 48, University of Chicago. The authors gave a battery of mental ability tests to 7th- and 8th-grade children in two Chicago-area schools. **The sample.** 301 students: 156 from Pasteur School and 145 from Grant-White School; ages roughly 11 to 16. We use all 301 together and ignore school (comparing schools would be a multi-group analysis, which comes later). **The measures.** nine, intended to measure three abilities: Visual (spatial), Textual (verbal), and Speed. | Variable | Test | Intended ability | |----------|------|------------------| | `x1` | Visual perception | Visual (spatial) | | `x2` | Cubes | Visual (spatial) | | `x3` | Lozenges | Visual (spatial) | | `x4` | Paragraph comprehension | Textual (verbal) | | `x5` | Sentence completion | Textual (verbal) | | `x6` | Word meaning | Textual (verbal) | | `x7` | Speeded addition | Speed | | `x8` | Speeded counting of dots | Speed | | `x9` | Speeded discrimination of straight and curved capitals | Speed | Other fields in the data: `id` (student ID), `sex` (1 = male, 2 = female), `ageyr` and `agemo` (age in years and months), `school` (Pasteur or Grant-White), `grade` (7 or 8). **Research question** (for this lab). > Among 7th and 8th graders, does **visual (spatial) ability** predict **textual (verbal) ability** and **processing speed**? Spatial reasoning is often thought to support general problem solving, so the working hypothesis is that students with higher visual ability also tend to score higher on both verbal tests and speeded tasks. This is a teaching question. The data are observational, so we will talk about *prediction*, not cause. --- # Setup ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} library(lavaan) library(semPlot) hs <- HolzingerSwineford1939 # Standard errors in this lab are bootstrapped (resampling the 301 students). # The seed makes your results reproducible; n_boot is the number of resamples. set.seed(625) n_boot <- 1000 ``` ::: # Step Anything surprising or potentially problematic? --- # Step 2: Measurement model (CFA) ## 2a. Write the model Three latent variables, each measured by its three tests. Remember that with `lavaan()` you must write out: - the loadings (fix the first loading of each factor to 1 to set its scale), - the **variance** of each latent variable, - the **covariances** among the latent variables, - the **residual variance** of every indicator. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # YOUR TURN model_cfa <- " # PLACEHOLDER (meaningless): delete these lines and write your measurement model x1 ~~ x1 x2 ~~ x2 x3 ~~ x3 x4 ~~ x4 x5 ~~ x5 x6 ~~ x6 x7 ~~ x7 x8 ~~ x8 x9 ~~ x9 x1 ~~ x2 # (gives the diagram something to draw) " ``` ::: ## 2b. Fit it and draw it ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} fit_cfa <- lavaan(model_cfa, data = hs, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = n_boot) # Did it converge? Any warnings above? lavInspect(fit_cfa, "converged") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} semPaths(fit_cfa, what = "std", style = "lisrel", layout = "tree", rotation = 2, residuals = TRUE, nCharNodes = 0, sizeMan = 8, sizeMan2 = 4, edge.label.cex = 0.9) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_rlab_cfa_to_lvpa_runbook_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 2c. Model fit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} fitMeasures(fit_cfa, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chisq df pvalue cfi rmsea 890.988 35.000 0.000 0.030 0.285 rmsea.ci.lower rmsea.ci.upper srmr 0.269 0.301 0.282 ``` ::: ::: Is the fit acceptable? State the criteria you are using (and where they come from), compare each index to them, and give your overall judgment. Indices can disagree: say how you weighed them. ## 2d. Parameter estimates ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Standardized loadings std <- standardizedSolution(fit_cfa, boot.ci.type = "perc") std[std$op == "=~", c("lhs", "rhs", "est.std", "se", "pvalue")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] lhs rhs est.std se pvalue <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Latent variable correlations lv <- c("visual", "textual", "speed") std[std$op == "~~" & std$lhs != std$rhs & std$lhs %in% lv, c("lhs", "rhs", "est.std", "se", "pvalue")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] lhs rhs est.std se pvalue <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Variance explained in each indicator lavInspect(fit_cfa, "rsquare") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` numeric(0) ``` ::: ::: What does this say about convergent and divergent validity? --- # Step 3: Modification indices (optional model change) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} modindices(fit_cfa, sort. = TRUE, maximum.number = 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: lavaan->modindices(): list with extra parameters is empty; to release equality constraints, use lavTestScore() ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] lhs op rhs group mi epc sepc.lv sepc.all [9] sepc.nox <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names) ``` ::: ::: Would you change the model? Look at the largest indices and decide: - Does the change make **theoretical** sense (not just statistical sense)? - Is it a measurement change (a cross-loading or residual covariance)? - If you decide **no change**, explain why. If **yes**, say exactly what you will add and why. If you make a change, write the revised model below (copy `model_cfa` and add your change). If you make no changes, leave the placeholder as is (it copies `model_cfa`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # YOUR TURN (skip if you made no changes) # If you make a change: replace the next line with a copy of model_cfa named model_cfa2 # plus your change. model_cfa2 <- model_cfa ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} fit_cfa2 <- lavaan(model_cfa2, data = hs, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = n_boot) fitMeasures(fit_cfa2, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chisq df pvalue cfi tli rmsea srmr 890.988 35.000 0.000 0.030 0.003 0.285 0.282 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Is the revised model a significant improvement? (Models must be nested.) anova(fit_cfa2, fit_cfa) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: lavaan->lavTestLRT(): some models have the same degrees of freedom ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chi-Squared Difference Test Df AIC BIC Chisq Chisq diff RMSEA Df diff Pr(>Chisq) fit_cfa2 35 8301.2 8338.2 890.99 fit_cfa 35 8301.2 8338.2 890.99 0 0 0 ``` ::: ::: Did the fit improve? Did the loadings change? Is the change worth keeping? Did you introduce anything strange (a negative variance, a loading that flipped sign)? --- # Step 4: Proceed to the structural model? Decision point. Decide which measurement model you are carrying forward (original or revised), and say whether you will proceed. A structural model can only be as good as the measurement model under it. If the measurement model were unacceptable, what would you do instead? --- # Step 5: Structural model (LVPA) ## 5a. Write the model Use the measurement model you decided on in Step 4 and add the structural paths that answer the research question. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # YOUR TURN model_sem <- " # PLACEHOLDER (meaningless): delete these lines and write measurement model + structural paths x1 ~~ x1 x2 ~~ x2 x3 ~~ x3 x4 ~~ x4 x5 ~~ x5 x6 ~~ x6 x7 ~~ x7 x8 ~~ x8 x9 ~~ x9 x1 ~~ x2 # (gives the diagram something to draw) " ``` ::: ## 5b. Fit it and draw it ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} fit_sem <- lavaan(model_sem, data = hs, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = n_boot) lavInspect(fit_sem, "converged") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} semPaths(fit_sem, what = "std", style = "lisrel", layout = "tree", rotation = 2, residuals = TRUE, nCharNodes = 0, sizeMan = 8, sizeMan2 = 4, edge.label.cex = 0.9) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_rlab_cfa_to_lvpa_runbook_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 5c. Model fit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} fitMeasures(fit_sem, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chisq df pvalue cfi tli 890.988 35.000 0.000 0.030 0.003 rmsea rmsea.ci.lower rmsea.ci.upper srmr 0.285 0.269 0.301 0.282 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Compare to the measurement model you carried forward. # (Use fit_cfa2 here instead if you revised the measurement model.) anova(fit_sem, fit_cfa) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: lavaan->lavTestLRT(): some models have the same degrees of freedom ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chi-Squared Difference Test Df AIC BIC Chisq Chisq diff RMSEA Df diff Pr(>Chisq) fit_sem 35 8301.2 8338.2 890.99 fit_cfa 35 8301.2 8338.2 890.99 0 0 0 ``` ::: ::: Is the structural model's fit acceptable? How does it compare with the measurement model's fit? Did the structural paths you added make the fit worse, and if so, by how much? ## 5d. Structural estimates ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Structural paths only: unstandardized and standardized est <- parameterEstimates(fit_sem, boot.ci.type = "perc", standardized = TRUE) est[est$op == "~", c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est", "se", "z", "pvalue", "ci.lower", "ci.upper", "std.all")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] lhs op rhs est se z pvalue ci.lower [9] ci.upper std.all <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Variance explained in the latent variables lavInspect(fit_sem, "rsquare")[c("textual", "speed")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA NA ``` ::: ::: Also check that the measurement part did not change meaningfully now that the structural paths are included. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} std_sem <- standardizedSolution(fit_sem, boot.ci.type = "perc") std_sem[std_sem$op == "=~", c("lhs", "rhs", "est.std", "pvalue")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] lhs rhs est.std pvalue <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names) ``` ::: ::: **Your response.** For each structural path, report the direction, size (standardized), and whether it is statistically distinguishable from zero. Interpret the variance explained. --- # Step 6: Answer the research question Briefly, answer the following based on the results: Among 7th and 8th graders, does visual ability predict textual ability and processing speed? Include: - the evidence (standardized paths, uncertainty, variance explained), - how confident you are, given the model fit, - at least **two limitations** (think about the design, the sample, the measures, and the model decisions you made). --- ::: {.content-visible when-profile="teacher"} # Teacher answer key *Stripped from the student download. Each answer is in its own collapsible box.* ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 2a: measurement model (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model_cfa <- " visual =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3 textual =~ 1*x4 + x5 + x6 speed =~ 1*x7 + x8 + x9 visual ~~ visual textual ~~ textual speed ~~ speed visual ~~ textual visual ~~ speed textual ~~ speed x1 ~~ x1 x2 ~~ x2 x3 ~~ x3 x4 ~~ x4 x5 ~~ x5 x6 ~~ x6 x7 ~~ x7 x8 ~~ x8 x9 ~~ x9 " ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 2c: fit interpretation (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chisq df cfi tli rmsea srmr 85.306 24.000 0.931 0.896 0.092 0.065 ``` ::: ::: df = 24 (45 observed moments minus 21 free parameters: 6 free loadings + 3 factor variances + 3 factor covariances + 9 residual variances). Chi-square = 85.3 on 24 df, significant (n = 301 makes the test sensitive). CFI = 0.931 and TLI = 0.896 are below the common .95 cutoff (CFI is near the looser .90 line); RMSEA = 0.092 exceeds .08 (poor/marginal); SRMR = 0.065 is under .08. Verdict: mediocre, not clearly acceptable. Accept any defensible, criteria-based judgment. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 2d: parameter estimates (teacher)"} Loadings are mostly strong (standardized roughly .4-.9; x1-x3 and x7-x9 are lower than the textual items). The factors correlate moderately (roughly .3 to .5), so they are distinct. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 3: modification indices (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` lhs op rhs mi epc 30 visual =~ x9 36.411 0.577 76 x7 ~~ x8 34.145 0.536 28 visual =~ x7 18.631 -0.422 78 x8 ~~ x9 14.946 -0.423 33 textual =~ x3 9.151 -0.272 55 x2 ~~ x7 8.918 -0.183 ``` ::: ::: Two large, interpretable options: - `x7 ~~ x8` (residual covariance, MI about 34): both are *speeded, paper-and-pencil arithmetic-like tasks*, so a shared method/format effect beyond the speed factor is plausible. This is the most conservative option. - `visual =~ x9` (cross-loading, MI about 36): x9 (discrimination of letter shapes) arguably draws on visual perception. Plausible, but it changes what the factors mean and is a bigger move. A strong answer picks one (or none) and justifies it substantively; weaker answers just cite the largest MI. Here we add the residual covariance. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 3: revised model and result (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model_cfa2 <- paste(model_cfa, "\n x7 ~~ x8\n") # i.e. model_cfa plus: x7 ~~ x8 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chisq df cfi tli rmsea srmr 53.272 23.000 0.966 0.946 0.066 0.047 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chi-Squared Difference Test Df AIC BIC Chisq Chisq diff RMSEA Df diff Pr(>Chisq) fit_a2 23 7487.5 7569.0 53.272 fit_a 24 7517.5 7595.3 85.305 32.033 0.32109 1 1.516e-08 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: The revised model improves fit (CFI = 0.966, RMSEA = 0.066, SRMR = 0.047) and the chi-square difference is significant. Remind students that the change is data-driven and should be reported as post hoc. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 4: proceed? (teacher)"} Proceed with the revised model (or the original, if justified): all loadings are significant and substantial and the factors are distinct, so the latent variables are measured well enough to relate to each other. If a factor were poorly measured, or fit were unacceptable and not fixable on theoretical grounds, stop and revisit measurement rather than interpreting structural paths. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 5a: structural model (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model_sem <- " visual =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3 textual =~ 1*x4 + x5 + x6 speed =~ 1*x7 + x8 + x9 textual ~ visual speed ~ visual visual ~~ visual textual ~~ textual speed ~~ speed textual ~~ speed x1 ~~ x1 x2 ~~ x2 x3 ~~ x3 x4 ~~ x4 x5 ~~ x5 x6 ~~ x6 x7 ~~ x7 x8 ~~ x8 x9 ~~ x9 x7 ~~ x8 " ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 5c: fit, and the saturation point (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chisq df cfi tli rmsea srmr 53.272 23.000 0.966 0.946 0.066 0.047 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: lavaan->lavTestLRT(): some models have the same degrees of freedom ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chi-Squared Difference Test Df AIC BIC Chisq Chisq diff RMSEA Df diff Pr(>Chisq) fit_s 23 7487.5 7569 53.272 fit_a2 23 7487.5 7569 53.272 -3e-10 0 0 ``` ::: ::: With the residual covariance `textual ~~ speed` **included**, the structural part is *saturated*: the two paths plus the residual covariance reproduce all three latent covariances, so the structural model has the **same df and exactly the same fit** as the measurement model (the `anova()` shows a chi-square difference of 0 on 0 df). Fit therefore says nothing about the paths; it only confirms the measurement model. If students **omit** the residual covariance, df rises by 1 and the model asserts that, after accounting for visual ability, textual and speed are uncorrelated. That is a testable claim; have them check the chi-square difference. Either choice is acceptable if justified and the df are explained. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 5d: structural estimates (teacher)"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` lhs rhs est se pvalue std.all 10 textual visual 0.511 0.099 0 0.457 11 speed visual 0.236 0.064 0 0.544 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` textual speed 0.2084932 0.2961692 ``` ::: ::: Visual ability predicts both outcomes. Standardized paths are about 0.46 (textual) and 0.54 (speed); both significant (p < .001). Visual ability explains roughly 21% of the variance in textual ability and 30% in speed, a moderate amount, leaving most variance unexplained. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Step 6: sample write-up (teacher)"} Yes, with caveats. Students with higher visual ability tended to have higher textual ability and faster processing speed (standardized paths about .5 each, both significant), and visual ability accounts for roughly 20-30% of the variance in each outcome. The measurement model fit was only marginal before one theoretically motivated modification, and the structural model inherits that. Limitations: (1) cross-sectional observational data, so these are associations rather than effects; (2) two schools pooled, ignoring school-level differences and clustering; (3) only three indicators per factor; (4) the residual covariance was added after looking at the data, so it should be replicated; (5) a single historical sample of 7th and 8th graders may not generalize. ::: :::
